title: Inputs and Outputs
description: Pass information into a function with arguments, and get a result back with return.

items: `cheer()` from the last lesson always did exactly the same thing.
Functions get far more useful when you hand them something to work with.
Write a name inside the `()` of the `def` line. That name becomes a variable that only exists **inside** the function.

content.concept: An argument going into a parameter
content.text: The envelope has a label: `name`. That is the **parameter**. The letter you put inside, `"Alex"`, is the **argument**. The function opens the envelope and uses whatever it finds.

items.title: Parameter
items.text: The name in the `def` line. A placeholder waiting for a value.

items.title: Argument
items.text: The real value you send in when you call the function.

content.code:
def greet_user(name):
    print("Hello, " + name + "!")

greet_user("Alex")
greet_user("Sarah")

steps.note: Python learns the function. Nothing runs yet.
A call with the argument `"Alex"`. Python jumps into the function.
The parameter `name` is filled with the argument.
The body uses `name`, so it prints the greeting for Alex.
Back outside, `name` is gone: it only lived inside the function. Now a second call, with `"Sarah"`.
A fresh `name` box, this time holding `"Sarah"`.
Same body, different value inside the box.

content.title: Watch the argument travel in
content.outro: The parameter gets a new value on every call.

content.question: In `greet_user("Sam")`, what is `"Sam"`?
content.explain: The value you send in when you call is the argument. The name in the `def` line is the parameter.

items: List several parameters, separated by commas.
Pass the same number of arguments when you call it.
**Order matters:** the first argument goes into the first parameter, the second into the second, and so on.

content.value:
def rectangle_area(width, height):
    print(width * height)

rectangle_area(4, 3)
rectangle_area(3, 4)
content.caption: Both print `12`, but in the second call `width` and `height` are swapped over.

content.value: Send different values into the machine below and watch each step. The row that matters is the second one, where the parameter takes the value you passed.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `10` goes into `a` and `3` goes into `b`, so the body works out `10 - 3`.

items: Printing an answer shows it once. Then it is gone: a dead end.
The `return` keyword **hands the value back** to whoever called the function.
The call is then replaced by that value, so you can store it in a variable.

content.text: You put something in, and the machine hands something back out into your hand. What you do with it next is up to you. `return` is the machine's tray.

content.code:
def double_number(number):
    return number * 2

result = double_number(10)
print(result)
print(result + 5)

steps.note: To work out the right side of `=`, Python must call the function. It jumps in with `10`.
`number * 2` is `20`. `return` hands `20` back and leaves the function.
Back at the call. It is replaced by `20`, which is stored in `result`. `number` is gone.
`result` really is a number, so you can keep using it: `20 + 5`.

content.title: Watch the value come back
content.outro: The returned value lands in `result`, ready to use again.

content.value: A function stops the instant it reaches `return`. Any lines after it inside the function never run. Remember this when a function seems to ignore its last few lines.
content.title: return ends the function

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `return` hands back `8` and leaves the function straight away, so the `print("Done")` inside never runs.
content.code:
def add_one(n):
    return n + 1
    print("Done")

print(add_one(7))

items: They can look the same on screen. They are **not** the same.
`print` **shows** a value and gives nothing back.
`return` **gives back** a value and shows nothing.

items.title: print
items.code:
def double(n):
    print(n * 2)

x = double(4)
print(x)
items.text: Shows `8`, then `None`. The function gave nothing back, so `x` holds `None`.

items.title: return
items.code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

x = double(4)
print(x)
items.text: Shows `8` once. `x` really holds `8`, so you can use it again.

content.title: Same look, different result
content.caption: Let the function work out the answer and `return` it. Then the code that called it decides: print it, save it, or feed it into something else. That keeps the function useful in more than one place.

content.value: Switch between `print` and `return` below and watch what the variable holds.

content.question: What does `x` hold after this runs?
content.explain: `show` prints `8` but has no `return`, so it gives nothing back. `x` ends up holding `None`.

full_name = make_full_name("Ada", "Lovelace")
print(full_name)

quiz.question: What do we call the values you pass into a function's parentheses?
quiz.explain: The values you pass in are arguments. The names waiting for them in the def line are parameters.

quiz.question: Which keyword sends a result back out of a function?
quiz.explain: `return` hands the value back so the rest of your program can use it. `print` only puts it on the screen.

quiz.question: What does 'total' hold?  def add(a, b):  /  print(a + b)  /  total = add(2, 3)
quiz.explain: The function prints 5 on screen but never returns anything, and a function with no return hands back None.
